national.title: Two European women held captive for more than a year in Niger freed in Libya
national.summary: The aid workers from Switzerland and Austria are due to fly home on Thursday, reports say.
national.body:
Two women - a Swiss and an Austrian – have been freed after more than a year in captivity in Niger and handed over to authorities in the Libyan city of Benghazi.

Austrian national Eva Gretzmacher, 76, and Swiss Claudia Abbt, 69, were kidnapped separately in the northern Nigerien city of Agadez in January and April last year.

No details have been given about who was holding them or their demands, although some reports have previously linked the kidnapping to Islamic State militants. The circumstances of their release were not disclosed.

Libyan officials were reported as saying the women would be handed over to authorities in their respective countries after necessary procedures were completed.

Libya's al-Masar TV showed the two women entering what looks like an ambulance and later being attended to by a health worker.

Speaking in French, the women thanked Khalifa Haftar, military commander of eastern Libya, and his son, Saddam Haftar, for their release.

Gretzmacher was an aid worker who had lived for many years in Niger, while Abbt had spent several years living and working as a community worker in Agadez.

A plane was expected to leave Benghazi on Thursday, first stopping in Vienna to transfer Gretzmacher to Austrian authorities before continuing to Switzerland with Abbt, privately owned Air Info Agadez news outlet reported.

national.title: U.S. reducing troop footprint in Middle East, sources say
national.summary: The U.S. military has quietly reduced its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats from Iran and its Houthis allies in Yemen, sources tell CBS News.
national.body: Saudi Arabia's state-owned Saudi Aramco, the world's biggest oil company, told staff to evacuate the company's headquarters in the eastern city of Dhahran and to work remotely, the Reuters news agency reported Thursday, citing six sources with knowledge of the matter. Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels have hit the kingdom repeatedly with missile and drone attacks in recent weeks. Last week a missile struck an Aramco building in Dhahran, which is on Saudi Arabia's Persian Gulf coast. The strike caused a "limited fire" at Saudi Aramco's headquarters complex, the kingdom's energy ministry said at the time.

national.title: Idaho mom who blamed vaccines for twins' deaths facing death penalty
national.summary: Andrea Shaw, 23, has said the 18-month-old twins became sick and died after receiving flu shots and routine childhood vaccinations.
national.body: An Idaho prosecutor is seeking the death penalty against a woman charged with murder in the 2025 deaths of her twin toddlers. Andrea Shaw, 23, has pleaded not guilty and has said the 18-month-old twins became sick and died after receiving flu shots and routine childhood vaccinations. But Payette County Prosecutor Mike Duke wrote in court documents that an autopsy revealed symptoms consistent with smothering and wrote that suffocation "is the only conceivable explanation" for their deaths.In July, a grand jury indicted Shaw, on two counts of first-degree murder, according to court records and a statement from the Payette Police Department.Deputy prosecuting attorney Ryon Sirucek notified the court of his intent to seek the death penalty last week. In the court document, Sirucek said the state would try to show that four aggravating factors make capital punishment appropriate in the case: That more than one murder was committed at the time; that the killings were especially heinous, atrocious or cruel; that the defendant showed "utter disregard" for human life; and that she would likely pose a continuing threat to society. "That's outrageous," said Shaw's attorney, Joseph Filicetti. "They're not going to be able to prove the underlying case beyond a reasonable doubt, so there's not a chance the death penalty is going to come into play."Filicetti requested the court drop the indictment against Shaw due to alleged improprieties in front of a grand jury, CBS affiliate KBOI-TV reported.He said the grand jury that indicted Shaw wasn't told that the county coroner found the cause of death to be undetermined but consistent with hyperthermia, or overheating. The pathologists who examined the twins also said their causes of death were undetermined, Filicetti said."A prosecutor has a duty of candor, meaning that they have to be truthful in front of [the grand jury] and they have a duty to provide exculpatory evidence, which is evidence giving [the grand jury] any reason to believe that this person's not guilty - some other reason that these deaths could have occurred outside of murder - and the prosecutor did not do that," Filicetti told KBOI. national.title: El Salvador's president threatens Haitian gangs over military hostages
national.summary: Four members of the so-called Gang Suppression Force have been missing since Sunday.
national.body:
El Salvador's president has said he has launched a military operation to rescue four air force personnel who have been missing in Haiti since Sunday.

Nayib Bukele wrote in a post on X that Wednesday's attack was "nothing" compared with what would happen if all the hostages - who he said were not combatants - were not returned alive.

They went missing after being ambushed by "heavily armed criminal groups," El Salvador's armed forces said. The ambush occurred in Croix-des-Bouquets, an area controlled by armed groups.

They were part of the so-called Gang Suppression Force (GSF), approved by the United Nations Security Council earlier this month, to tackle escalating gang violence in Haiti.

According to Bukele, the mission consisted of pilots and technical personnel, whose primary jobs were to "carry out medical evacuations and save lives, not to wage war".

His post said the Salvadoran military operation's single objective was to bring the four men back home alive.

He added that if all four were returned alive, without being harmed, "everything will go back to how it was before the kidnapping".

Bukele added they were kidnapped "in a cowardly manner" while returning after buying food at a market in the area.

national.title: Celebrity shark guided out of South Korea canal refuses to swim out to sea
national.summary: Bukangi the shark became an unlikely sensation after it was spotted in a canal in Busan weeks ago.
national.body:
A famed dusky shark in South Korea is still lingering near a canal that it was guided out of on Wednesday.

The shark, nicknamed Bukangi, became an unlikely sensation after it was spotted swimming in a canal in the south-eastern port city of Busan last month. For weeks, rescuers tried in vain to get it back to the open sea using large nets.

On Thursday, authorities said they had reinforced barriers to prevent Bukangi from returning. But it has yet to swim out into the open sea, and has been circling back repeatedly to the mouth of the waterway.

Its rescue prompted mixed reactions in Busan, where some said the shark should stay while others felt it was better for it to go.

In a livestreamed operation on Wednesday, rescue workers took more than eight hours to delicately guide the three-metre-long (10ft) shark with a net towards open water in a harbour.

Hundreds of adoring fans gathered at the park overlooking the canal, cheering and waving goodbye to the shark.

But then, on Thursday morning, Bukangi reportedly swam back into the canal after breaking through a barrier installed by authorities.

For some time, Bukangi was trapped in a tight space between two layers of nets in the canal.

national.title: Nigeria's first Ebola patient holidayed in Uganda, officials say
national.summary: The wife of a diplomat based in Abuja travelled to Kampala for a vacation.
national.body:
Nigeria's first confirmed case of Ebola since the outbreak in East Africa began in May is the wife of a diplomat who travelled to Uganda's capital for a holiday, the head of Africa's health agency has told the BBC.

The woman is originally from Uganda but based in Abuja, where she fell ill three days after arriving home in the Nigerian capital on 3 October, according to Dr Jean Kaseya from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention.

Nigeria's health minister has confirmed to the BBC the 42-year-old patient spent two and a half weeks in Kampala, adding that she also made a two-hour stopover in Ethiopia's capital on her return.

The authorities were working to prevent the virus from spreading and had identified 44 people who had been in contact with the woman, who tested positive for Ebola on Tuesday, the minister said.

"Not all of them have been in close proximity. We cast the net wide so that we contain it as broadly as possible," Pate told the BBC.

Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo said 46 people - 44 who had come into contact with the woman at hospital and two people who worked in her home - had been banned from boarding flights.

Nigeria has also stepped up Ebola surveillance at its international airports following confirmation of its first case in more than a decade, he said.

Measures include health screenings, temperature checks, tracking travellers' movements and digital health declarations, Mr Keyamo said.

national.summary: President Trump is set to rally with Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa as he seeks to boost GOP candidates in a political environment that has dimmed for the party — prompting pushback from some candidates, including Hinson.
national.body: Sioux City, Iowa — President Trump is set to rally Thursday with Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa as he seeks to boost Republican candidates in a political environment that has dimmed for the party — prompting modest pushback from the very candidates he's supporting.Hinson, who is running for Iowa's open Senate seat, initially pledged to be the president's "top ally" in the upper chamber. But as she faces off against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek in a contest that, like several in the Hawkeye State, has grown more competitive than expected, she's adjusted that commitment in recent weeks. When she and Turek went head-to-head at a debate earlier this month, the former local news anchor said she would be Mr. Trump's ally when it's "important for Iowa." But she said she would "push back on him" when it's needed — as she said she would regardless of who's in the White House. Last week, Hinson told Fox News: "If he's going to say something that's wrong, I'm going to challenge him on it." "I'm not afraid to say, 'hey, I disagree with you on this,'" she said. "But I'll be an ally to somebody when they're with me."For Republicans, the Senate race in Iowa is just one of several in which Democrats appear competitive despite Mr. Trump winning the state by double digits in 2024. Iowa has been hit hard by high energy prices and last year's U.S.-China trade war, which led Beijing to boycott American soybeans. It's a picture that appeared unthinkable at the outset of the cycle — and puts Republicans' Senate majority on the line. Hinson, who's represented the state in the House since 2021, said she would be at the rally on Thursday to welcome Mr. Trump to Iowa, "because I think this is a contrast election." national.title: Police investigate Married at First Sight Australia after 'inappropriate' allegations
national.summary: New South Wales Police say inquiries took place "following a report of inappropriate content being shared".
national.body:
Married at First Sight Australia is facing fresh controversy after police launched an investigation into the hit reality TV show.

New South Wales told BBC News that inquiries had taken place "following a report of inappropriate content being shared".

Channel Nine, which broadcasts Married at First Sight Australia, confirmed that it was "aware of a police investigation" involving the show's production company.

It is the latest blow for the show, after a BBC News investigation earlier this year into MAFS Australia revealed cast members said they had not been told their partners had previous drug and violence convictions.

Those revelations led to a warning from Australia's media watchdog, which called them "serious and disturbing".

The British version of Married at First Sight, known to many as MAFS UK, was separately plunged into crisis in May after BBC Panorama reported rape allegations from two female cast members - allegations the men involved have denied.

MAFS UK is made by a different production company to the Australian version.

Panorama investigates allegations that raise serious concerns that welfare procedures on Married at First Sight UK have failed contributors, leaving them at risk of harm.

national.title: How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders?
national.summary: Many view it as one of the most pivotal elections in Israel's history, with global implications.
national.body:
Israel's general election takes place on Tuesday 27 October.

It's the first election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel and its subsequent conflicts in Gaza and with Iran, Hezbollah and the Houthis.

Many view it as one of the most pivotal elections in Israel's history, with global implications.

Current polling puts incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu in a tight race with Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israel Defense Forces, to become prime minister.

Eisenkot's popularity stems partly from his military credentials and his relative newness in politics, having formed his Yashar Party only last year.

He lost his son, a soldier, in the first months of the Gaza war, and served in Israel's war cabinet under Netanyahu until resigning in 2024 over disagreements about the conflict. He has built his campaign on calls for accountability over the security failures that led to 7 October.

Other opposition leaders include former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman - both right-wingers who take hardline positions on security and advocate permanent Israeli control over much of the occupied West Bank - and Yair Golan, a left-winger who supports Israel's withdrawal from large parts of the territory. Despite their differences, they could work with Eisenkot to form a government.

Netanyahu's current government is the most right-wing in Israel's history. In order to remain in power, he will likely have to rely on the support of some of his existing far-right coalition partners. Some hold ultra-nationalist positions, such as calling for Israel to annex the West Bank and for the "migration" of Palestinians from Gaza - which could amount to the forced displacement of civilians. Some members of Netanyahu's own Likud party have also called for Palestinian "migration" from the territory.

national.title: Two killed in attack on airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, authorities say
national.summary: It is the latest in a series of attacks by the Houthi movement which have targeted airports and other sites in the kingdom.
national.body:
Two people were killed and eight others injured in an attack on an airport in Dammam, eastern Saudi Arabia on Wednesday evening, the kingdom's General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) says.

Those killed at King Fahd International Airport were a Saudi citizen and an Indian resident, while the injured were Saudi, Indian, Yemeni, Bangladeshi and Nepalese nationals.

The GACA did not say what type of attack occurred, but Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement has repeatedly targeted the kingdom's airports with drones and missiles.

On Wednesday morning, two people were killed by debris from a drone that was intercepted over Eastern Province, where Dammam is located, the Saudi energy ministry said.

The ministry said the drone was intercepted as it attempted to target a processing facility owned by Saudi Arabia's state oil company Aramco in the Shaybeh oil field, where a contractor's vehicle was set ablaze.

It identified the dead as residents from the Philippines and Nepal.

Another four drones were also intercepted on Wednesday night, according to the Saudi-led coalition that is supporting the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis.

There was no immediate comment from the Houthis, but they have previously said they are attacking Saudi airports, energy facilities and military bases in retaliation for deadly Saudi air strikes on the territory they control in western Yemen.

national.title: Some New Yorkers back ban on horse-drawn carriages, but drivers fear for incomes
national.summary: As councillors prepare to banish the vehicles, views in Central Park are divided over the 160-year-old tradition.
national.body:
After petting a carriage horse in New York's Central Park at the age of five, Alexus Lawson was hooked.

She has driven a carriage in Manhattan's most famous park, pulled by her horse, for six years. But since Lawson heard about the city's vote this week to outlaw the carriages over animal and public-safety concerns, she has been worried.

"What am I supposed to do with my horse?" asked the 28-year-old, who has been driving in the park for six years. "You're going to tell me I can't work with her anymore? How am I supposed to ensure her health?"

Lawson is one of roughly 200 horse-drawn carriage drivers in Central Park. Use of the carriages has been an at-times controversial tradition for over 160 years that has become a popular tourist activity.

On Thursday, New York City Council is expected to vote to pass a ban on the carriages that would start in June 2028. The proposal is backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who says he will help develop a transition plan for workers in the industry.

But several drivers who spoke to the BBC said they did not want new jobs, and disputed claims their horses are mistreated - even as many New Yorkers and tourists welcomed the ban.

Horse-drawn carriages in New York City expected to be outlawed

Published 13 October "There were a few cases of horses dying in the middle of the park. You can clearly see that they're not taken care of," said New York resident Ron Tsur. "That's not what they're supposed to be doing."

national.title: 5 simple ways to relieve the aches and pains of sitting at a desk all day
national.summary: Sitting at a desk all day hurts. And it isn't good for us. Strategies to make it a little more comfortable, from eye muscle exercises to alleviate eye strain to a back pain-fighting body movement.
national.body:
If you sit in front of a computer for long periods of time, whether it's for work or leisure, you've probably experienced one of these symptoms.

But there are ways to relieve some of this discomfort — and even combat some of the health risks that may come with prolonged sitting. That includes walking breaks, ergonomic solutions and quick, simple stretches.

Here's a roundup of tips that have been previously featured on Life Kit.

But there may be a way to mitigate its harms. In 2023, researchers at Columbia University Medical Center set out to find the least amount of movement you need to counteract the dangers of prolonged sitting. And they found that walking for five minutes every 30 minutes was the most effective strategy .

In 2023, our colleagues at NPR's Body Electric tested out this five-minute walking exercise on our NPR listeners. Over 20,000 participants joined the challenge — and reported higher productivity and lower fatigue .

Want to give this walking challenge a try? Get instructions from Body Electric — and use this worksheet to keep track of your walking breaks .

Beck Harlan/NPR Anyone who works at a desk knows how easy it can be to slip into a slouch. If we're not careful, that mid-back rounding can creep into all of our sitting time and create pain by putting stress on the middle section of our spine.

This movement above seeks to relieve that stress and encourage flexibility by mimicking the natural movements of the spine — side bending, bending backward and rotating, says Vinh Pham, a physical therapist. The idea is to get the body comfortable with these motions so that when you encounter them in real life, they're not painful.

national.title: A GOP congressman voted to cut Medicaid. It covers 62% of his district. Can he win?
national.summary: Republican U.S. Rep. David Valadao is fighting for reelection in central California. 6 in 10 residents of his district are covered by Medicaid, which he voted to cut last year.
national.body:
Rep. David Valadao, R-Calif., leaves the stage after speaking at a campaign event in Bakersfield, Calif. on Sept. 30, 2026. Jae C. Hong/AP hide caption

Ulises Hernandez, of Bakersfield, Calif., has had health coverage through Medicaid for as long as he can remember.

But he had never waited as long for care as he did in September after a dental crown slipped down his throat during a procedure. He spent eight hours in an emergency room waiting for care and more than two days without food.

This story was produced in partnership with KFF Health News .

Sitting in his wheelchair to protest looming federal Medicaid cuts outside Republican U.S. Rep. David Valadao's Bakersfield office, Hernandez described his wait as a foreshadowing of what's ahead.

"I couldn't eat, I couldn't drink, I couldn't do anything, and I was in pain," said Hernandez, who had been discharged from the hospital a few days before. "I'm livid."

Hernandez, 41, said Valadao "should be ashamed of himself" for voting for the Republicans' One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The law is expected to reduce Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion through 2034, with provisions such as stricter Medicaid eligibility rules and reducing federal money to states.

Hernandez plans to vote for challenger Randy Villegas in hopes that this Central Valley toss-up district, where roughly 6 in 10 of constituents are enrolled in Medicaid, can help give Democrats control of Congress.

national.title: Trump's redistricting gave Republicans a head start, now it goes to the voters
national.summary: President Trump, seeking to reshape the voting map, prompted a rare wave of mid-decade redistricting that gave Republicans a boost for holding the House. But the voters will determine if it works.
national.body:
Voters across much of the South are casting ballots ahead of next month's midterm elections in congressional districts that were redrawn following calls from President Trump. He said it would help the GOP hold the House, where they currently outnumber Democrats 218 to 214 .

In state legislatures over the last year, Republicans tilted about eight more seats their way than Democrats did in response. (That's an estimate, shown on the bar graph below.)

Here's the catch: Republicans redrew districts partly on how people voted in the presidential election in 2024. Now the political mood has changed and many who voted for President Trump two years ago could be voting for Democrats, or not voting, in the midterms. The Republicans could lose many of the districts they targeted.

Usually, states redistrict early in each decade after the census. But Trump called on legislatures to do it now. It set off a chain reaction of political crises across the country that threw legislatures into the national spotlight.

Elections See how new voting maps in Texas and California shift the political landscape Texas Republicans issued arrest warrants for Democratic legislators who'd left the state. The Louisiana governor suspended a primary after thousands of votes were already cast so the lines could be redrawn. In Missouri, the state supreme court found the Republican secretary of state in contempt for sticking with a GOP map that was not legally in effect.

Elections How predominantly Black areas in 6 states have been split up by redistricting In California and Virginia, Democrats won approval in statewide votes for redistricting in response to the Republicans in other states – only to have the courts toss out Virginia's plan. And when the Supreme Court weakened the Voting Rights Act this spring, it fueled rushed legislative sessions to draw maps that often ended up weakening the voting power of minority communities .

In a few places, Republicans rejected Trump's call to redistrict, including dramatic votes in the Indiana and South Carolina legislatures. But overall, Trump prompted a cycle of mid-decade redistricting unlike any since the 1960s , when courts set the current rules.

national.title: How long does it take to save up for a starter home? Twice as long as it did in 2019
national.summary: A new analysis finds that the average renter household now needs 16 years to save for a down payment and closing costs. Rising rents and other costs have consumed a growing share of household budgets.
national.body:
Mortgage rates topping 7% is the latest sign of how hard it has gotten to buy a first house, with aspiring owners already facing sky-high prices. A new analysis out Thursday shines a light on yet another growing obstacle: the amount needed to close a home loan.

"Over the last seven years, the time to save up that down payment and closing costs has doubled," said Mike Calhoun, president of the Center for Responsible Lending, a research nonprofit that promotes economic opportunity. The report was released by the center's Julian Bond Institute .

Since 2019, the last time the center made the same calculation, home prices have shot up, inflation spiked and has remained stubbornly high, and the rising cost of food, gas, healthcare and more has strained family budgets. Closing costs on a home loan have also ticked up, driven in part by rising homeowners insurance.

Only on NPR Voters here will decide whether to force cities to build cheaper, smaller homes Economy It's getting harder to afford rent in the U.S., even for middle-income families Amid all this, renters' incomes have not kept pace, and personal savings rates have dropped.

Today, the center calculates that for a median-income renter household, it would take a "staggering 16 years" to save up a down payment and closing costs for a starter home. That's twice as long as in 2019. And it would take even more time — 21 years — for a median-income Black renter household.

That kind of time frame upends a main reason that many look to buy in the first place. As the analysis notes, "young children at the time the family starts saving may have left the household — for higher education or the workforce — before the family will have saved enough to purchase their first home."

The report also narrows its calculations to middle-income households — making roughly $50,000 to $120,000 — whose members are more likely to be viable homeowners. For them, the savings time has also doubled, to 12 years.

For front-line workers, such as police officers, firefighters, EMTs, nurses and teachers, the researchers find that "the years to save has at least doubled and now ranges from 10 to 13 years."

national.title: Trump merchandise stores are closing: 'He has peaked'
national.summary: At least four Trump merchandise stores have closed this year. Store owners say with Trump in his final term, there isn't as much to fire up his consumer fan base and sales have softened.
national.body:
The Trump Store in Bensalem, Pa., a Philadelphia suburb, closed early this year amid falling sales. Frank Langfitt/NPR hide caption

BENSALEM, Pa. – When the Trump merchandise store here announced it was closing earlier this year, Wes Alker, a Trump superfan and retired auto mechanic, came by for some nostalgia and the going-out-of-business deals. They included everything from "Trump Won" caps for $9.99 to Trump pool floats for $19.99.

Trump stores first emerged during the 2016 campaign. But with the president now in his second and final term, store owners say there isn't as much to fire up the consumer fan base and sales have softened.

At least four stores have closed this year. The MAGA Mall , a big online retailer and wholesaler, reports sales of MAGA gear are down 30% compared to a presidential election year when Trump is on the ballot.

Trump fans Wes Alker and Joseph Flanagan pose at a going-out-of-business sale at a Trump store in suburban Philadelphia. Flanagan lives nearby and said he visited the store more than 25 times. Frank Langfitt/NPR hide caption

"He's no longer a viable business model for entrepreneurs because he has peaked," said Alker, who wore a gray T-shirt with a photo of former President Joe Biden and former Vice-President Kamala Harris which read, "Dumb and Dumber."

Trump's lame duck status isn't the only drag on demand. When the Bensalem store closed – it still maintains an online presence – Trump's average approval rating had already fallen from 50 % when he took office to 44 %.

Nine months later, when Bill Hays shut down his Trump super store outside of Knoxville, Tennessee, the president's approval rating had fallen five more points.

national.title: Farm country has beef with Trump as midterms approach
national.summary: President Trump's attempts to bring beef prices down has potentially backfired politically in several key states.
national.body:
Driving around his farm in a four-wheeler, Scott Birker warned that his cattle were in a bad mood.

When asked why, he said matter-of-factly: "We just got done weaning."

Birker should know his herd well, given that he's been raising beef cattle outside the Eastern Iowa town of Garrison since 2001. His operation has about 150 "mama cows" and sells feeder calves, as well as some cattle for meat. And Birker is also the northeast regional vice president for the Iowa Cattlemen's Association.

All of which is to say that since August, when Trump announced that his administration would raise the quota on beef imported under lower tariffs – temporarily suspending tariffs on up to 300,000 metric tons of imported beef – Birker knows it when he says: that hurt people.

"That surprise, with a very volatile market already, with a tight supply, hurts us really, really fast and really, really hard," Birker said.

It's not that raising beef cattle was easy before that new import policy. Margins are always tight, says Zach Raff, incoming livestock economist at Iowa State University. But there have also been other challenges – for example, drought in much of the western U.S. made hay much more expensive and shrank the nation's beef herd.

"The beef herd size is at an all time low – a 75-year-low," said Raff. "So you couple that with very strong demand. And that's going to make prices what you see at the store right now."

Ground beef currently costs around $6.80 a pound – a fact of which the Trump administration is keenly aware. But the administration's attempts to bring those prices down have backfired politically and possibly economically..

national.title: See how Big Tech is transforming Spain's landscape
national.summary: A drought-stricken region of northeast Spain has become a focus for American companies searching for locations to place their data centers.
national.body:
ZARAGOZA, Spain — Aragon's rugged plains stretch out under a clear blue sky, the buildings visible as "a few tiny cubes sprawled like a throw of dice" across the terrain — as George Orwell wrote in Homage to Catalonia, of his time here during the Spanish Civil War in the 1930s. Today, excavators eat the earth, carving huge chunks of the landscape in the race to build the behemoths of the AI boom.

This drought-stricken region of northeast Spain has become the focus of American companies searching for locations to place their energy- and water-intensive data centers. In Aragon, Amazon Web Services promises to spend almost $40 billion to build multiple vast complexes — one alone as large as 600 American football fields. Microsoft and the asset management firm Blackstone are among those following suit, signing agreements to build data centers that will transform this region and the livelihoods of its inhabitants.

Heavy equipment excavates an area adjacent to an Amazon data center currently under construction in Cuarte, Spain, on Sept. 29. Local authorities have approved dozens of data center projects for U.S. Big Tech and other companies that will transform the character of this region. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption

Even as other countries enact regulations to curb the expansion of data centers (and Spain's national government weighs new restrictions), Aragon's regional government is welcoming the companies with open arms. Touting themselves as the "Virginia of southern Europe" after the U.S. state with the largest concentration of data centers, they are taking the bet that hosting data centers will bring jobs and prepare the region for the economic shifts they believe AI will bring.

"This is a new economy that is evolving, and it's very difficult to foresee how many activities are going to be coming around it," said Eva Valle, the economic counsellor for the regional government. "But they are coming."

national.title: Trump merchandise stores are closing: 'He has peaked'
national.summary: At least four Trump merchandise stores have closed this year. Store owners say with Trump in his final term, there isn't as much to fire up his consumer fan base and sales have softened.
national.body:
The Trump Store in Bensalem, Pa., a Philadelphia suburb, closed early this year amid falling sales. Frank Langfitt/NPR hide caption

BENSALEM, Pa. – When the Trump merchandise store here announced it was closing earlier this year, Wes Alker, a Trump superfan and retired auto mechanic, came by for some nostalgia and the going-out-of-business deals. They included everything from "Trump Won" caps for $9.99 to Trump pool floats for $19.99.

Trump stores first emerged during the 2016 campaign. But with the president now in his second and final term, store owners say there isn't as much to fire up the consumer fan base and sales have softened.

At least four stores have closed this year. The MAGA Mall , a big online retailer and wholesaler, reports sales of MAGA gear are down 30% compared to a presidential election year when Trump is on the ballot.

Trump fans Wes Alker and Joseph Flanagan pose at a going-out-of-business sale at a Trump store in suburban Philadelphia. Flanagan lives nearby and said he visited the store more than 25 times. Frank Langfitt/NPR hide caption

"He's no longer a viable business model for entrepreneurs because he has peaked," said Alker, who wore a gray T-shirt with a photo of former President Joe Biden and former Vice-President Kamala Harris which read, "Dumb and Dumber."

Trump's lame duck status isn't the only drag on demand. When the Bensalem store closed – it still maintains an online presence – Trump's average approval rating had already fallen from 50 % when he took office to 44 %.

national.title: How long does it take to save up for a starter home? Twice as long as it did in 2019
national.summary: A new analysis finds that the average renter household now needs 16 years to save for a down payment and closing costs. Rising rents and other costs have consumed a growing share of household budgets.
national.body:
Mortgage rates topping 7% is the latest sign of how hard it has gotten to buy a first house, with aspiring owners already facing sky-high prices. A new analysis out Thursday shines a light on yet another growing obstacle: the amount needed to close a home loan.

"Over the last seven years, the time to save up that down payment and closing costs has doubled," said Mike Calhoun, president of the Center for Responsible Lending, a research nonprofit that promotes economic opportunity. The report was released by the center's Julian Bond Institute .

Since 2019, the last time the center made the same calculation, home prices have shot up, inflation spiked and has remained stubbornly high, and the rising cost of food, gas, healthcare and more has strained family budgets. Closing costs on a home loan have also ticked up, driven in part by rising homeowners insurance.

Only on NPR Voters here will decide whether to force cities to build cheaper, smaller homes Economy It's getting harder to afford rent in the U.S., even for middle-income families Amid all this, renters' incomes have not kept pace, and personal savings rates have dropped.

Today, the center calculates that for a median-income renter household, it would take a "staggering 16 years" to save up a down payment and closing costs for a starter home. That's twice as long as in 2019. And it would take even more time — 21 years — for a median-income Black renter household.

That kind of time frame upends a main reason that many look to buy in the first place. As the analysis notes, "young children at the time the family starts saving may have left the household — for higher education or the workforce — before the family will have saved enough to purchase their first home."

The report also narrows its calculations to middle-income households — making roughly $50,000 to $120,000 — whose members are more likely to be viable homeowners. For them, the savings time has also doubled, to 12 years.

For front-line workers, such as police officers, firefighters, EMTs, nurses and teachers, the researchers find that "the years to save has at least doubled and now ranges from 10 to 13 years."

national.title: Trump's redistricting gave Republicans a head start, now it goes to the voters
national.summary: President Trump, seeking to reshape the voting map, prompted a rare wave of mid-decade redistricting that gave Republicans a boost for holding the House. But the voters will determine if it works.
national.body:
Voters across much of the South are casting ballots ahead of next month's midterm elections in congressional districts that were redrawn following calls from President Trump. He said it would help the GOP hold the House, where they currently outnumber Democrats 218 to 214 .

In state legislatures over the last year, Republicans tilted about eight more seats their way than Democrats did in response. (That's an estimate, shown on the bar graph below.)

Here's the catch: Republicans redrew districts partly on how people voted in the presidential election in 2024. Now the political mood has changed and many who voted for President Trump two years ago could be voting for Democrats, or not voting, in the midterms. The Republicans could lose many of the districts they targeted.

Usually, states redistrict early in each decade after the census. But Trump called on legislatures to do it now. It set off a chain reaction of political crises across the country that threw legislatures into the national spotlight.

Elections See how new voting maps in Texas and California shift the political landscape Texas Republicans issued arrest warrants for Democratic legislators who'd left the state. The Louisiana governor suspended a primary after thousands of votes were already cast so the lines could be redrawn. In Missouri, the state supreme court found the Republican secretary of state in contempt for sticking with a GOP map that was not legally in effect.

Elections How predominantly Black areas in 6 states have been split up by redistricting In California and Virginia, Democrats won approval in statewide votes for redistricting in response to the Republicans in other states – only to have the courts toss out Virginia's plan. And when the Supreme Court weakened the Voting Rights Act this spring, it fueled rushed legislative sessions to draw maps that often ended up weakening the voting power of minority communities .

In a few places, Republicans rejected Trump's call to redistrict, including dramatic votes in the Indiana and South Carolina legislatures. But overall, Trump prompted a cycle of mid-decade redistricting unlike any since the 1960s , when courts set the current rules.

national.title: Farm country has beef with Trump as midterms approach
national.summary: President Trump's attempts to bring beef prices down has potentially backfired politically in several key states.
national.body:
Driving around his farm in a four-wheeler, Scott Birker warned that his cattle were in a bad mood.

When asked why, he said matter-of-factly: "We just got done weaning."

Birker should know his herd well, given that he's been raising beef cattle outside the Eastern Iowa town of Garrison since 2001. His operation has about 150 "mama cows" and sells feeder calves, as well as some cattle for meat. And Birker is also the northeast regional vice president for the Iowa Cattlemen's Association.

All of which is to say that since August, when Trump announced that his administration would raise the quota on beef imported under lower tariffs – temporarily suspending tariffs on up to 300,000 metric tons of imported beef – Birker knows it when he says: that hurt people.

"That surprise, with a very volatile market already, with a tight supply, hurts us really, really fast and really, really hard," Birker said.

It's not that raising beef cattle was easy before that new import policy. Margins are always tight, says Zach Raff, incoming livestock economist at Iowa State University. But there have also been other challenges – for example, drought in much of the western U.S. made hay much more expensive and shrank the nation's beef herd.

"The beef herd size is at an all time low – a 75-year-low," said Raff. "So you couple that with very strong demand. And that's going to make prices what you see at the store right now."

Ground beef currently costs around $6.80 a pound – a fact of which the Trump administration is keenly aware. But the administration's attempts to bring those prices down have backfired politically and possibly economically..

national.title: What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble?
national.summary: AI uncovered long-hidden programming flaws, triggering a rare global cyber-security response.
national.body:
For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet.

It took artificial intelligence (AI) to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert.

The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites.

Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout of the discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline.

Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI.

OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".

Most people may not have heard of PHP, but they probably interact with it daily.

Short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, it powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress – the content management system behind many websites like blogs.

national.title: How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election
national.summary: Disaffection has often driven down turnout among Arab Israelis, but there is a strong push to get rid of the right-wing governing coalition.
national.body:
At rush hour in Nazareth, the largest Arab-majority city in Israel, students are handing out leaflets by the roadside urging motorists to vote in next week's closely fought, general election. Polls indicate that Arab parties could be left holding a critical balance of power.

Disaffection has often driven down past turnout among Arab Israelis - who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. But this election, there is a strong push to get rid of the most right-wing governing coalition in the country's history - an alliance between veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.

"I see it as our duty to bring down this extremist government. They treat us as second-class," says Arkan Badran, 23, who is with the students giving out flyers. "I call on all young men and women to vote for Arab lists, which represent us, because this is our future."

Most opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu and his partners nor the main "Change Bloc", led by centre-right former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a parliamentary majority.

If they are right, after the election anti-Netanyahu parties wanting to form a governing coalition would either have to go back on pledges not to work with the prime minister or make a deal with Arab-majority lists.

A major sticking point is that Eisenkot has so far ruled out forming a government with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values.

Israel's politics and society have been changed by the deadly, unprecedented Hamas-led assault on the country on 7 October 2023, and subsequent war in Gaza. There is increased mistrust of and hostility towards the country's Arab minority.

"After October 7, we were treated as enemies of this country," says Suha Salman Mousa of the Mossawa Centre in Nazareth, which advocates for equal rights for Arab citizens. "There was shrinking space for freedom of speech. There were major arrests, there was also firing of people from their workplaces because they put something on social media or they went out against the war on Gaza."

national.body: A massive chemical leak in Toledo, Ohio, is forcing some people out of their homes while others have been told to shelter in place.A plume of smoke full of chemicals erupted from the MC Tank terminal. national.title: US embassy accuses Canada of election meddling ahead of midterms
national.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney dismissed the claim, noting that US initiated trade actions against Canada.
national.body:
The US Embassy in Ottawa has accused Canadian officials of election meddling ahead of the November midterms.

The embassy said Canadian leaders have brushed off concerns over "potential interference", and that ministers and premiers "openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances".

Canadian leaders, including Prime Minister Mark Carney, have dismissed the claims. Relations between the North American neighbours have hardened during the second Trump administration.

The midterms will determine which political party controls both branches of the US Congress, which could have a significant impact on the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.

The fact sheet released by the US Embassy on Wednesday alleges the Canadian government "brushes off concerns about potential interference in U.S. elections, even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances".

It cites comments and actions, like meetings with US Democrats and calling for retaliatory tariffs against the US.

For example, it says that when Industry Minister Mélanie Joly was asked what she expected regarding tariffs if Democrats were to win midterm elections, she responded, "That's exactly why I'm meeting so many governors and potential presidential candidates."

Ontario Premier Doug Ford pushed Canada's federal government, it states, to consider additional retaliatory tariffs on imports from "politically significant states to the current administration's base of support".

national.summary: How much AI is too much when it comes to finding love on the apps? "It's very subtle," one dating app user said of his AI-enhanced photos.
national.body: Marissa, a 31-year-old Boston resident, downloaded dating apps because she is looking for love. But more and more, she finds herself looking for something else: AI-free photos.The marketing professional said she routinely comes across dating app profiles that appear to be digitally altered. Usually, the changes are minor and can be easily made using tools like Photoshop, such as editing someone out of a photo. Sometimes, however, the photo appears to be completely AI-generated, she told CBS News, citing a photo she came across on Bumble of a man dressed in a suit tiling a bathroom wall. "AI aside, I'm not sure what the appeal is there," she said (Marissa asked to withhold her surname for privacy reasons).Numerous women on TikTok also report spotting photos of men on dating apps that appear to be AI-generated. Their accounts demonstrate how AI is blurring the line between what's real and what's fake in the already fraught arena of online dating. They also raise ethical questions about how far is too far when it comes to manipulating your online persona."People want authentic connections and conversations," Kathryn Coduto, an assistant professor at Boston University who studies dating apps, told CBS News in an email. local.summary: Rochester teachers are preparing to hold a no confidence vote on Superintendent Eric Rosser over what the union leader calls a pattern of "reckless mismanagement" in the City School District.
local.body:
Listen • 1:13 Rochester teachers are preparing to hold a no confidence vote on Superintendent Eric Rosser over what the union leader calls a pattern of "reckless mismanagement" in the City School District.

This comes as contract talks between the administration and Rochester Teachers Association have reached an impasse, with a median session scheduled for Tuesday.

"Teachers are clamoring for a vote of no confidence," RTA President Adam Urbanski said. "And I'm saying, 'Okay, give it a little time,' because we want to see if mediation helps. We want to see if (Rosser) joins at the bargaining table in mediation.

"And if he doesn't, then we'll have no recourse but to do something like a vote of no confidence."

Concerns go beyond contract negotiations and a labor agreement that expired in June. Rosser's administration also has not adequately addressed teachers' concerns over student support needs and school safety, Urbanski said. School safety also was at the core of the union’s last no confidence vote back in 2021 involving then-Superintendent Lesli Myers-Small.

When the union surveyed its members in June, hundreds of teachers responded that they do not feel supported by the district and don’t think Central Office understands what is happening in classrooms, according to survey results Urbanski shared.

"If that's not an indictment, I don't know what it would be," Urbanski said. "This district is swimming in money. ... And yet they're skimping on services for English language learners and for special education children."

In a September email exchange between Urbanski and Rosser, obtained by WXXI News, Rosser wrote that there was "significant confusion" regarding the negotiation team's responsiveness to the union, adding that he would continue to "assess progress made to secure a successor agreement."

local.title: New urgent care proposed in Honeoye Falls targets unmet need. Some residents are pushing back
local.summary: The facility to be built on North Main Street would be leased and operated by F.F. Thompson Hospital.
local.body:
Construction is scheduled to start within the next month on a new medical facility in the village of Honeoye Falls that officials said is much needed in that area.

The 10,000-square-foot space will provide family medicine and urgent care services under the operation of Canandaigua’s F.F. Thompson Hospital, part of the UR Medicine network.

“The largest deficit of primary care is in the Honeoye ZIP code,” said Kurt Koczent, chief operating officer of Thompson Health. “The closest urgent care is in Henrietta, and it's about a 20-minute drive. ... This is exactly what a community hospital should be doing.”

This will be the village’s first urgent care center with extended hours, walk-in treatments, and on-site diagnostic services. The address will be 20 North St., which was once a restaurant and has since been abandoned.

Developer Pike Construction is seeking tax breaks and incentives valued at $750,000, or 21% of the estimated $3.6 million project cost — which the company has argued is necessary to offset construction cost inflation. Criticism during an hour-and-a-half-long public hearing last week focused on the veracity of those claims of financial need, and on the tax breaks, specifically a 14-year property tax abatement on the facility.

If the property were transferred to F.F. Thompson, the hospital is a nonprofit and the property would be fully exempt. The facility is expected to employ 26 full-time staffers.

Among those voicing concerns during the public hearing was village resident Cara Briggs.

“This is a very small town and a very small village absorbing the cost of something that is benefitting an area much larger than us, and bringing increased traffic, et cetera, in a town that has one stoplight. And we like that, by the way. One stoplight. Little traffic,” said Briggs, a local attorney who also serves as town justice for the town of Mendon, which encompasses Honeoye Falls.

The Town of Arkwright has approved a
local.body:
ARKWRIGHT -- Back in July, when the Town of Arkwright first discussed the idea of offering a tax exemption to veterans, Supervisor Brian McAvoy called it "the right thing to do." A couple months later, his fellow Board members took action to share that sentiment.

The Town of Arkwright has approved a real property tax exemption for military veterans by local law. Councilman Larry Ball, a U.S. Army veteran, recused himself from the vote, while the rest of the Board approved the local law.

After an inquiry from a resident, McAvoy could not come up with a good reason why not to offer a tax exemption to veterans. McAvoy sought clarity on the potential impact on the town, and after a discussion with Assessor Jeanne Ebersole, McAvoy came to the conclusion that offering a tax exemption to veterans would not be a significant expense for the Town of Arkwright.

McAvoy said it could end up being more of a "ceremonial" gesture than a major benefit to veterans, but that any exemption is worth pursuing. Ball said that as a veteran himself, he feels it is the principle of the decision that matters most.

Municipalities have three levels of exemptions that can be made available to veterans, including disabled veterans, combat veterans, and "Cold War Veterans", applying to all unnamed wars. Each exemption is capped at a certain amount, then equalized.

Depending on a veteran’s classification, they can expect a reduction of $21 to $107 in their Arkwright town taxes, commencing in 2028. The Assessor's Office will be reaching out to the town’s veterans to remind them to apply before March 1, 2027.

Veterans exemptions have been available since 1984, but it took until now for Arkwright to adopt a local law permitting veterans in the town to take advantage. McAvoy lamented that the Town did not adopt the exemptions earlier in his six-year tenure as Supervisor, but was pleased it could be done now.

Instead of shifting the additional tax burden to the remaining residents of the town, McAvoy stated that there is enough money in the reserve accounts to cover the difference. McAvoy wants to use the Town's existing funds and revenue streams, such as the wind turbine revenue, to account for the impact of any veterans tax exemptions.

Faez Elias Tayar, age 85, of Portland, NY, passed away on October 17, 2026. He was born on November 25, 1940, in Safita, Syria, and lived a life marked by hard work, generosity, and devotion to his family and community.

Faez came to be known as a man who could do just about anything with his hands and his heart. He took journeyman and trade classes in Syria, building the foundation for a lifetime of skilled work and practical knowledge. He later became self-employed in heating, plumbing, and electric work, operating Tayar Heating Plumbing and Electric in Portland, New York. Through his business, he earned the respect of many for his reliability, his strong work ethic, and his ability to solve problems with skill and determination.

He was a people person in every sense of the word. Faez was outgoing, entertaining, and always ready with a story or a warm welcome. He had a generous spirit and a natural way of making others feel comfortable. He especially enjoyed feeding everyone who came over, and he was known as someone who always took care of others before himself. His home was a place of hospitality, laughter, and good company, and those who knew him will remember the kindness and warmth he shared so freely.

Faez also enjoyed the simple pleasures of life. He liked hunting, fishing, and splitting wood, and he found satisfaction in staying active and useful. These interests reflected the same steady and dependable nature that guided him throughout his life. He took pride in honest work and in the everyday moments that brought people together.

He is survived by his wife, Dawn Babcock; his children, Tara and her husband, Matt Benware, Renee and her husband, Dave Popielarz Jr., and Jeffrey and his wife, Brynn Tayar; and his grandchildren, Courtney Popielarz, Hailey Popielarz, Zachary Popielarz, Chase Popielarz, Galen Benware, Kayden Benware, Hannah Tayar, and Colin Tayar. He is also survived by his brother, Maher and his wife, Suzy Tayar; his sister, Najwa Tayar; and many nieces, nephews, and cousins who will cherish his memory.

He was preceded in death by his parents, Elias and Mediha Tayar, and by his siblings, brothers, Odel and Majed, sisters, Nashere, Najoud, Najat, and Nejla. Their memories remained an important part of his life and family history.

Faez will be remembered for his strong presence, his generous heart, and the care he showed to everyone around him. He lived with purpose, worked with pride, and loved deeply. His family and friends will hold close the many memories of his humor, his hospitality, and the steady example he set throughout his life.

local.body:
ATLANTA (AP) -- Angel Reese had 21 points and 12 rebounds to help the Atlanta Dream beat the Golden State Valkyries 97-71 on Wednesday night and take a 2-1 lead in the WNBA Finals.

Rhyne Howard added 16 points and Naz Hillmon had 15 for the Dream, who host Game 4 on Saturday.

It was the second straight strong game for Reese, who had 30 points and 16 rebounds in Game 2, which the Dream also won for their first victory ever in the finals. She now has a double-double in each game of the Finals.

“It feels good when you’re in the finals. It’s a long season and you play against everybody and go through and push through, but when you can do it at the highest level, this is what you live for, this is what the offseason is for,” Reese said. “I put the work in for this moment and I’m just happy I could lead the team to a win. We’re feeling good going into Saturday.”

With the game tied at 49 in the third quarter, Atlanta scored eight straight, including four by Reese. Golden State got within 59-55 on Tiffany Hayes’ layup, but could get no closer as Atlanta closed the quarter scoring 12 of the final 14 points.

Atlanta has dominated the third quarter so far in the series, outscoring Golden State 63-35 combined in the three games.

With Atlanta up 17 in the fourth quarter, Jordin Canada overthrew Reese on the break, but she saved the ball by throwing it over her head underneath the basket to Howard, who got fouled.

local.summary: The Jamestown and Chautauqua County Democratic Party committees are asking Charles Nazzaro, a former Chautauqua County legislator who retired in 2021, to replace Vince DeJoy as the county legislator representing District 9 residents in Jamestown. DeJoy, who submitted his resignation as the District
local.body:
The Jamestown and Chautauqua County Democratic Party committees are asking Charles Nazzaro, a former Chautauqua County legislator who retired in 2021, to replace Vince DeJoy as the county legislator representing District 9 residents in Jamestown.

DeJoy, who submitted his resignation as the District 9 legislator on Thursday, Oct. 15, is moving to North Carolina where he has a new job.

DeJoy's name will remain on the ballot. Nazzaro will serve if DeJoy wins the election.

"We were surprised by Vince DeJoy's announcement," said Marcia Westling Johnson, county Democratic Party chairwoman. "We are excited to have a well-respected public servant and civic-minded person such as Chuck Nazzaro to stand in if DeJoy receives the winning number of votes. It is a short time to voting. We are optimistic that District 9 residents will vote for DeJoy on the ballot knowing that they will be getting Nazzaro as their legislator."

Nazzaro was first elected to the county legislature in 2008 and served for 14 years. He was a Jamestown City Council member before his election to the legislature. Nazzaro chaired the legislature's Audit and Control Committee when either the Democrats or the Republicans controlled the body.

"Chuck is well-regarded by both parties and respected for his budgeting knowledge," said Westling Johnson. "He was the chief financial officer at WCA Hospital for many years. We know he can have an impact on the legislature and county government from the get-go because of his vast knowledge and experience. "We know that DeJoy's resignation a mere week before ballots are being cast presents a real challenge. DeJoy is moving too late to change the ballot, but voting for DeJoy legally allows Nazzaro to step in."

The announcement was made during the Chautauqua-Cattaraugus Library Association’s annual meeting held recently. More than 100 librarians, library staff members, board of
local.body:
CELORON – Three north county libraries will share a $40,000 state grant to implement the Capable and Connected Caregivers program.

The announcement was made during the Chautauqua-Cattaraugus Library Association's annual meeting held recently. More than 100 librarians, library staff members, board of directors, trustees and supporters of the Chautauqua-Cattaraugus Library Association attended the meeting.

"A $40,000 grant is being shared by the Ahira Hall Memorial Library (Brocton), Dunkirk Public Library, and Darwin R. Barker Library," said Janice Dekoff, association executive director. "CCLS is acting as the financial agent to facilitate the transmission of funds from CRCF to the libraries."

The Capable & Connected Caregiving program meets these caregivers where they already are -- in their local libraries -- and gives them practical training, peer connection, and ready-to-use resources. Piloted across three geographically and demographically distinct Chautauqua County libraries, this program is designed to be replicable, community-owned, and built to last beyond any single grant cycle."

A CCLA report shows that in Chautauqua County, 17% of residents live below the federal poverty line, higher than the New York State average of 13.7%. Additionally, none of the three pilot communities have licensed, center-based infant and toddler slots. Nationally, 32.7% of grandparents living with grandchildren under age 18 serve as their primary caregivers.

"Across Chautauqua County, thousands of children are in the care of people who didn't set out to be caregivers --teens watching siblings after school, grandparents stepping in full-time, and library staff receiving children without the tools to engage them," Dekoff said. "In communities like Brocton, there are zero licensed childcare centers and only two small home daycares, both at or near capacity. Informal caregiving isn't a gap in the system. It is the system.

Dekoff said that the new program aims to deliver training, resources, and peer support through three programs hosted at local libraries:

-Teen caregivers can take part in hands-on workshops at local libraries with first aid, CPR and AED certification; emotional regulation skills, safe snack prep, allergy and medication awareness, as well as resume ready credentials and peer connection.

local.summary: The projects are part of a $10 million revitalization effort paid for by the state and the Ralph C. Wilson Foundation.
local.body:
Storefronts along West Main Street in Rochester are getting a refresh, part of a $10 million revitalization effort.

Among those slated for an upgrade are Morse Lumber and Busy Bee Restaurant . Grant funds also will help repair and reopen shuttered buildings along the corridor between Genesee Street and South Plymouth Avenue, including prepping the space immediately to the west of Busy Bee for a future café.

A total of 22 projects have been awarded grants ranging from $25,000 and $250,000 to cover up to 90% of eligible expenses. Funding for the project comes from New York state and the Ralph C. Wilson Foundation.

"This investment reflects what’s possible when government, philanthropy, businesses, and community organizations come together around a shared vision," Mayor Malik Evans said in a statement.

Evans joined others for a ceremonial groundbreaking on Wednesday outside Rochester Jewels , a nonprofit mentoring organization at 174-178 W. Main St. serving school-aged girls. That building is getting roof and window repairs. Grants also can be used for machinery and equipment, and improvements to public spaces. There are developing plans for public art and amenities to be added to the area, which officials said could leverage additional funding.

Busy Bee Restaurant, which has been downtown since the 1930s, and at its 124 W. Main St. location since the 1980s, will celebrate its grand re-opening on Monday. The building is slated to get a refreshed storefront and awning, as well as other work on the masonry, windows and drainage, while the upper floors are prepped for housing. Morse Lumber will see similar facade, siding and window improvements, pressure washing, painting and new signage, officials said.

entertainment.body:
Avatar star Stephen Lang is reuniting with director Uli Edel 37 years after Lang’s breakthrough performance in Edel’s Last Exit to Brooklyn .

Lang, who plays Colonel Miles Quaritch in James Cameron’s Avatar franchise, has signed on to star in The Mercy Rider , a modern-day Western thriller which Edel will direct from a script by Richard Julian.

Lang plays Joe McCabe, a former soldier and reclusive Texas rancher who decides to risk everything to fight back against immigration authorities after they detain a hardworking local father. Determined to reunite the farmer with his family, McCabe comes up against a hard-line immigration agent, Harvey “Hawk” Walters, played by Irish actor Jack Hudson . The film is set to shoot in Mexico. G. Mac Brown, a line producer on Last Exit , and an executive producer on Martin Scorsese’s Oscar-winning The Departed , and Neil Burger’s 2017 hit The Upside , will produce The Mercy Rider with Hudson.

entertainment.summary: The audio streaming giant reported its third-quarter results.
entertainment.body:
Monthly active users (MAUs) grew to 788 million, up from 777 million in the previous quarter and in line with the firm’s forecast. Spotify had guided to slower MAU growth in the third quarter, pointing to changes to products in emerging countries to help the company better monetize its user bases. Revenue growth for the quarter came in at 16 percent, or 14 percent on a constant currency basis, to get the company to €5.0 billion ($5.6 billion), matching its forecast. Operating income hit €672 million ($754 million) in the third quarter, with management guidance having called for €670 million. The figure was up 15 percent despite a 26 percent operating expenses increase, “primarily driven by an increase in marketing alongside cloud and AI spend in support of growth initiatives.” Related Stories Movies How 'Hanging by a Wire' Turned Pakistan's Daring Cable Car Rescue Into a Real-Life Thriller Business StudioCanal CEO on Chasing Gen Z Audiences: "There's Just No Room For Error"

Spotify touted that it gross margin and operating income came in ahead of expectations.

Profitability has been in the investor spotlight after price increases and cost cuts. Spotify shares rose more than 3 percent in early pre-market trading.

“This was a quarter where we did what we said,” said co-CEO Alex Norström. “We’ve built a strong business that keeps compounding, we invest when we see a path for growth, our costs are moderating, and there is more runway ahead.”

He added: “Spotify not only enjoys industry-leading engagement, but we also have the most passionate and engaged music, podcast and book fans in the world on our platform. That’s why we continue to grow and take share. Every time we expand what’s on Spotify, we bring in new listeners and give existing ones more reasons to come back, almost every day.” And co-CEO Gustav Söderström said: “Spotify is in one of the few categories that actually stands to thrive in the agentic age. This is because agents excel at replacing and taking care of things people would rather not do. People love getting rid of chores. But entertainment is the opposite. Nobody asks an agent to “summarize a song” for them. The whole point of getting rid of those chores is to free up even more time for the things that you actually enjoy.” For the current fourth quarter, Spotify predicted 316 million premium subs and 818 million MAUs, as well as operating income of €820 million and revenue of €5.2 billion.

entertainment.title: Amy Winehouse Honored With Stunning All-Star Tribute Concert Celebrating 20 Years of ‘Back to Black’: Best Moments
entertainment.summary: Jorja Smith, FLO, Sasha Keable and more took joined Amy's original band at the show at London's Roundhouse in Camden.
entertainment.body:
Camden has always belonged to Amy Winehouse . “This is her house,” Mark Ronson declared from the Roundhouse stage on Wednesday night (Oct. 21), and in the borough that raised her, where she is immortalized in photographs and has her very own statue, nobody was inclined to argue. The one-night-only celebration of Back to Black’ s 20th anniversary paid homage to a north Londoner turned global phenomenon, drawing a packed-out room just a short walk from the pubs where she first made her name.

The venue carried a weight of its own. Her 2003 debut Frank won over London’s jazz and R&B crowds, but it was also here that Winehouse made her final public appearance in July 2011, joining her goddaughter Dionne Bromfield on stage at the iTunes Festival; she died three days later, aged 27, from accidental alcohol toxicity.

While the essence of the songwriting was rooted in Camden, the sound of Back to Black was found in Brooklyn. It was at the Dap-Kings’ all-analogue Daptone Studios that Winehouse and producers Ronson and Salaam Remi landed on a brassy, jazz club grandeur that defined the record.

Released on Oct. 27, 2006, the album peaked at No. 2 on the Billboard 200 and won five Grammys. In the U.K., it ranks among the best-selling albums of all time, with more than 4.6 million chart units to date. America took to her, too, from SXSW to a 2007 Coachella set where, as Dap-Kings saxophonist Neal Sugarman recalled to Billboard U.K., she was “the toast of the festival.”

On Wednesday, Ronson and Remi reunited with the Amy Winehouse Band, led by longtime musical director Dale Davis, to play the album in full, with BBC Radio 2 DJ Jo Whiley hosting. Guest vocalists were hand-picked by the producers, with Paul O’Duffy, p*nut and former Island Records president Darcus Beese OBE also involved in the booking. The concert will be aired on U.K. television this Saturday (Oct. 24).

The line-up ranged from established names ( Corinne Bailey Rae , Jorja Smith , Lianne La Havas, Yebba, Jessie Reyez , Terri Walker) to newer voices (Nia Smith, Skye Newman, Sasha Keable ), with Baby Rose and FLO also on the bill. Beforehand, Remi had said he was curious to see “what these ladies bring to their versions” of the songs. They delivered: there wasn’t a dodgy Stars in Their Eyes impression in sight, just a feel-good procession of women reimagining Winehouse as she would have wanted. These were the best moments from the show.

Operating margin is one measure of the operational leverage the company’s executives can drive elsewhere in the business.

Operating expenses rose by about 26% in the third quarter from a year ago to 967 million euros ($1.1 billion), or 19% when Spotify accounts in constant currency and strips out payroll taxes related to its employees’ share-based compensation, which it calls social charges. entertainment.title: ‘Musk’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Show How Tell-All Docs Break Through Amid Industry Woes: MIA
entertainment.summary: Films like A24's buzzy Elizabeth Holmes documentary that pull the curtain back on fame and tabloid scandals are what’s working in global markets, the MIA Market in Rome heard on Thursday.
entertainment.body:
The box office success of A24’s You Can See Everything, the documentary about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes from directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, underlines what’s working for doc producers these days, the MIA Market in Rome was told on Thursday.

“It’s only celebrities, or if you have a really good investigative story, that will sell. Preferably when Beyonce does the narration,” Lea Fels, partner and co-owner of Dutch documentary maker Scenery, told a panel on indie doc making. Factual films that pull the curtain back on fame or tabloid scandals are all the rage with audiences in the global marketplace. Related Stories Movies Neon Will Distribute 'NAZA,' Providing a Major Boost and Seal of Approval Movies '14th' Leads Critics Choice Documentary Awards Nominations

These include Oscar winner Alex Gibney ‘s four-hour dissection of Elon Musk , Disney’s intimate Oasis reunion movie, NAZA , the politically charged Gaza documentary from Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, and the ICE documentary They’re Here from Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller.

Anna Godas, CEO of U.K.-based Dogwoof, said content aimed at streamers or U.S. buyers is a major consideration for her production banner, as our films about the lives and experiences of celebrities. “Unless it’s crime, or someone famous, it’s not going to work. That’s the reality at this point,” she explained.

To navigate an industry-wide malaise for documentary producers brought on by industry consolidation and budget contractions, Dogwoof is experimenting with bite-sized non-fiction films structured like micro dramas, and on YouTube with A Coffee With… series. “I love that someone can come and see a documentary and not be subject to gatekeepers, who are limiting what people can see,” Godas argued.

Stephanie Carter, an executive producer with THIRTEEN, the New York-city based PBS station, said selling documentaries is less a concern for her platform than the loss of funding after the Trump administration in Washington, D.C. pulled indirect funding to NPR and PBS in 2025 amid a conservative backlash.

“We lost our funding, which was sad, and we spent the past year coming up with a new financial model,” Carter explained. That means attaching a distributor to series content, or THIRTEEN investing some of its own funds to keep a series going.

Of course, times of political and economic turmoil leave doc producers having to weigh making films that can find audiences and making films a company really believes in. “Everytime it’s a challenge. But as a producer, do the projects you feel need to be told, but be realistic as a company of the results. And find partners,” Fels argued.

entertainment.title: Chappell Roan Brings Out Christina Aguilera at L.A. Concert: ‘Honestly Paved the Way for Me’
entertainment.summary: Aguilera performed "Beautiful" at the Super Graphic Spectacular concert before joining Roan for a duet of the latter artist's track "Coffee."
entertainment.body:
On the first night of Chappell Roan ‘s Super Graphic Spectacular in Los Angeles, the star had a “Coffee” date with an icon.

About midway through Roan’s set on Wednesday (Oct. 21), the singer-songwriter brought out surprise guest Christina Aguilera , who went on to belt a gorgeous rendition of her 2002 hit “Beautiful” before joining Roan in a duet of the latter’s Midwest Princess track “Coffee.”

“I want to introduce this person [who] honestly paved the way for me and all women in pop to do whatever the f–k they want, sing and wear whatever the f–k they want…and I’m so grateful to have her,” Roan said from the stage at L.A.’s Shrine Auditorium before introducing Aguilera. “She’s a f–king legend.”

After hugging Roan and taking the mic, Aguilera offered her own praise for the younger star, stating, “From the moment I heard Chappell’s voice, I knew she was a force to be reckoned with.” She then launched into a pitch-perfect rendition of “Beautiful” as Roan looked on.

The pair subsequently dueted on “Coffee,” which Aguilera described as “one of my favorite songs of hers.” A visibly flustered Roan initially flubbed the opening line — eliciting a good-natured laugh from Aguilera — but quickly recovered and beautifully traded off verses with her pop elder before the two harmonized together for the song’s finale. You can watch video of the duet here .

During her set, Roan also performed a rendition of Olivia Rodrigo ‘s “Expectations,” which the two released a remix of last week. She was preceded on stage by openers Lola Young , Tinashe , Amanda Lepore, Blaine Petrovia and Kyra Jeté.

Wednesday was night one of the two-night Spectacular, which continues Thursday (Oct. 22) with another headlining set by Roan along with performances by openers Caroline Polacheck , MUNA , Alisa Mae, Fantasia Royale Gaga and Sweaty Eddie.

All proceeds from the concerts will be donated to Roan’s Midwest Princess Project , which has raised more than $800,000 to date for over 60 organizations benefiting trans youth and LGBTQ+ communities.

Canal+ on Thursday posted total revenue for the first nine months of 2026 of €6.41 billion ($7.20 billion), up 37.5 percent, driven by the acquisition of African pay-TV giant MultiChoice. Excluding MultiChoice, revenue was up 1.3 percent to €4.65 billion ($5.22 billion).
